title: AI and ageing are being framed as an inclusion and agency problem across health, economic security, participation and connectivity
source_unit: ITU, Artificial intelligence and ageing: Inclusive pathways for older persons in a digital world
geography: Older persons globally, with attention to age, gender, regional, affordability, skills, trust and connectivity differences

observations.period: 2026 publication; AI and later life domains

denominator.unit: key domains identified on the ITU publication page

health.value: the report examines how AI shapes health and wellbeing in later life

economic_security.value: the report examines AI and economic security for older persons

participation.value: the report examines participation and connectivity as part of inclusive ageing in a digital world

observations.method: ITU publication combining global evidence, lessons from practice and recommendations for stakeholders and decisionmakers; jointly developed with EY and KAIST.
observations.uncertainty: The public publication summary does not provide a single global estimate of AI use or outcome effects among older persons.
observations.subgroup: Older persons, older women, people in developing regions, caregivers, health and social-care providers, employers, technology firms and public institutions.
observations.counterinterpretation: AI can support access and autonomy while also increasing surveillance, dependency, error exposure, cost or exclusion when human support and non-digital alternatives decline.

observations.period: 2026 publication; unequal distribution of AI benefits

denominator.unit: intersecting inequality dimensions highlighted by the publication

age.value: the distribution of AI benefits differs across older and younger age groups

gender.value: gender differences are identified as shaping access to AI benefits in later life

region.value: regional differences are identified as shaping the distribution of AI benefits for older persons

observations.method: Global evidence and practice lessons synthesized through an age- and gender-responsive digital-inclusion lens.
observations.uncertainty: The summary identifies unequal distribution but does not quantify the size or causal source of each gap across countries.
observations.subgroup: Older women and men, urban and rural older persons, people in high- and low-resource regions, people with disabilities and people with different household support.
observations.counterinterpretation: Age, gender and regional gaps may interact with income, education, disability, language, health, household support, trust and service design rather than operate independently.

observations.period: 2026 publication; pathways to narrow the AI divide

responsibility.value: the report recommends responsible, inclusive and human-centred AI for ageing societies

capacity.value: narrowing the AI divide is linked to stakeholder action, practice lessons and inclusive design rather than technology availability alone

participation.value: AI is positioned as something that should support older persons’ inclusion, participation and wellbeing across the life course

observations.method: Practice-informed global policy publication developed with ITU, EY and KAIST.
observations.uncertainty: Recommendations are not an implementation inventory, intervention effect estimate or guarantee that human-centred design will reach the most excluded older people.
observations.subgroup: Older persons, families, caregivers, technology designers, governments, civil society, health systems and service providers.
observations.counterinterpretation: Inclusive design can improve usability while leaving affordability, care capacity, data governance and institutional accountability unresolved.

observations.period: 2026 public webinar and publication framing; barriers to participation

denominator.unit: intersecting barriers identified in ITU public materials

barriers.value: age, gender, geography, digital access, affordability, skills and trust are identified as intersecting barriers to AI participation for older persons

design.value: age- and gender-responsive approaches and digital literacy are presented as conditions for inclusive AI participation

partnerships.value: cross-sector partnerships are emphasized as necessary to ensure older persons benefit from digital transformation

observations.method: Publication summary and ITU webinar materials presenting preliminary findings, practice examples and expert discussion.
observations.uncertainty: The webinar and public summary are not a representative survey or outcome evaluation; barrier categories do not show how many older people face each one.
observations.subgroup: Older persons with limited connectivity, income, skills, trust, language access or family and institutional support, especially older women and people in developing regions.
observations.counterinterpretation: Digital literacy and better design help, but they cannot alone resolve unequal income, inaccessible care systems, labor-market exclusion, discrimination or privacy risk.

related_sources.claim: ITU webinar page describing preliminary findings, collaborators and practice discussions.
ITU digital-inclusion program context for older persons and inclusive participation.

boundary: This record adds an ageing and digital-inclusion route linking AI to health, economic security, participation, connectivity, age and gender inequality, affordability, skills, trust, human support and institutional design. It is a global policy publication and practice synthesis, not a representative older-person survey, clinical or financial outcome study, causal AI evaluation, implementation inventory or proof that AI improves later-life wellbeing.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official ITU publication page and related webinar materials were reviewed for the four later-life domains, unequal age/gender/regional distribution, responsible and human-centred pathway, barriers, digital literacy and cross-sector partnership claims.
